summary: KilnWorks is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for latency-sensitive document-summarization and redaction pipelines. Main concerns: strict tenant isolation, burst behavior during batch job spikes, KMS integration, and cost predictability. Redwood AE + SE walked through reserved node sizing, warm-pool/prewarm, fallback to hosted tiers, and preliminary benchmark plan. Next: pricing, benchmark scope, and compliance docs.
transcript:
[00:00] Alex (AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Alex from Redwood - I'm here with Priya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Jordan (CTO): Good, thanks. Busy week but glad we could make time.
[00:10] Priya (SE): Hi all, quick note - we'll go over capacity needs and then dive into any security questions. Feel free to interrupt.
[00:18] Maya (Platform Eng): Sounds good. We're mainly focused on dedicated capacity for production inference - low tail latency for our document redaction flow.
[00:25] Ethan (SRE): Yeah, we have nightly batch jobs too that create spikes - so burst is a real concern.
[00:32] Alex: Great, can you give us a rough sense of QPS and model sizes?
[00:36] Jordan: Right now we're averaging 120QPS during daytime peak for the summarization model, but the nightly job spikes to about 2k concurrent requests for a short window, may be 10-20 minutes. Model is a 16B gombert - uh Gompel? sorry, 16 billion parameter open model variant, quantized to int8 in prod later.
[01:02] Priya: Got it. So two patterns - steady sustained throughput and short high-concurrency bursts. We usually recommend a reserved pool sized for steady state and a warm pool or burst capacity for the spiky windows, with autoscale rules.
[01:15] Maya: How deterministic is the warm pool? We can't afford cold starts at 99th percentile.
[01:20] Priya: That's our main engineering focus - warm pool (hotpool) prewarm ensures KV cache and model weights are resident. We can pre-allocate hot nodes and keep them partially warm; there's tradeoffs in cost. For strict tail latency you want some dedicated hot replicas.
[01:35] Rosa (Security): On the security side we need tenant isolation - we cannot have noisy neighbors. We also require KMS integration and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
[01:44] Alex: We support VPC-only private deployments and an on-prem path if needed. For KMS we integrate with major providers (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, HashiCorp Vault). We also provide per-tenant RBAC and audit trails.
[01:58] Jordan: Do you have SOC2?
[02:00] Alex: Yes, SOC2 Type II and ISO mention in the doc pack - we can share those.
[02:05] Ethan: What's the fallback if reserved pool saturated? Do you route to hosted instances?
[02:11] Priya: We can configure policy-based fallback. Options: spill to Redwood hosted (if data residency and compliance allow), fall back to a smaller quantized variant pinned to the same tenant, or implement queueing with SLA cutoffs. We walked through this with a customer last quarter.
[02:26] Jordan: Hmm, we likely need the fallback to stay within our VPC. Is there a private-to-hosted data egress concern?
[02:33] Alex: If you require strict VPC isolation, we offer private deployments with a private control plane; fallback can be to pre-provisioned reserved nodes in another AZ or private cluster. No egress to hosted unless you opt in.
[02:45] Maya: About sizing - with 120QPS steady and spikes to 2k, how would you recommend sizing?
[02:51] Priya: Quick rule of thumb: model latency x QPS gives CPU/GPU concurrency needs. For a 16B at ~120ms token latency (varies), for steady 120QPS you'd want N GPUs; for bursts we recommend a warm pool sized for 20-30% of peak plus auto-burst headroom. But we prefer to build a concrete benchmark with your payloads.
[03:14] Jordan: What's the billing model for reserved vs burst?
[03:18] Alex: Reserved capacity is committed monthly/annual. Burst consumption can be billed as overage or via burst credits depending on contract. We'll include both flavors in the pricing sheet.
[03:27] Maya: Any concerns about our model being quantized? We already run int8 in staging.
[03:32] Priya: That's fine; runtime supports int8/4-bit paths. Quantization will reduce memory pressure and improve throughput, which helps with warm pool density. We'll capture that in the perf run.
[03:44] Ethan: For the nightly batch spike, we could also temporarily route to a higher throughput variant, but that risks quality differences.
[03:51] Alex: Right, quality tradeoffs are something we flag in Redwood Optimize - you can configure auto-fallback thresholds that keep quality within an allowed delta.
[03:59] Jordan: How long to spin up additional nodes if autoscale? We can't wait 5 minutes for the nightly window.
[04:05] Priya: Cold scale can be slow. That's why warm pools exist; autoscale is for progressive scaling. Warm pool ensures sub-second or low-second readiness. We can model prewarm timelines in the benchmark.
[04:18] Rosa: Also need to confirm key rotation flows with KMS — we need HSM-backed keys for PII redaction.
[04:25] Alex: We can support HSM-backed keys via customer KMS or BYOK. We'll capture integration patterns in the security pack.
[04:33] Maya: Any limitations on prewarming many different model versions/variants? We sometimes run multiple checkpoints for A/B.
[04:40] Priya: Prewarming many variants increases memory overhead; we recommend pinning a small set of canaries and using KV cache warming for less-used versions. For A/B you can prewarm the canary and use fast cold-start techniques for the rest.
[04:55] Jordan: What about network egress costs between AZs if we do a cross-AZ fallback?
[05:00] Alex: We can architect to minimize cross-AZ egress; if everything stays in your VPC we can co-locate. We'll include cost modeling in the pricing doc.
[05:08] Ethan: We have a compliance window next month and need to ensure any pilot doesn't break audit controls. Can we limit logs retention?
[05:16] Rosa: We want audit logs forwarded but masked and retention configurable.
[05:20] Priya: That is configurable per account; retention and masking rules can be set and logs forwarded to your SIEM endpoint.
[05:27] Jordan: OK. For the benchmark, we'll provide a sample of 1,000 typical requests and the nightly batch payload. What's the turnaround?
[05:34] Priya: We'll scope the benchmark and estimate 2-3 business days for an initial run once we have samples. We'll run steady state and spike scenarios and provide p50/p95/p99 latency and cost per 1k tokens.
[05:46] Alex: I'll also share a short playbook that shows prewarm sizes and a recommended reserved config for your profile.
[05:52] Maya: Are there any vendor lock-in risks with private deployment?
[05:56] Alex: The private control plane is designed to be portable; models and configs are standard artifacts. There's some operational overhead but we support exportable configs and model version pins.
[06:06] Jordan: Competitors question — we looked briefly at Anthropic and our own fleet. Why pick Redwood?
[06:12] Priya: Two things — production runtime optimizations (KV caching, batching, prewarm) and unified ops across hosted/dedicated/private so you don't rewrite your stack. We also offer SLOs and enterprise support.
[06:24] Ethan: Any SLA numbers you can share now?
[06:28] Alex: Typical dedicated SLAs cover uptime and latency SLOs in contracts. We'll include the SLA examples in the packet.
[06:34] Jordan: Sounds good. Let's talk timeline — we need pilot running before end of next month if possible.
[06:40] Alex: That's doable pending benchmark results and contract. We'll aim to have pricing and benchmark scope out by Friday.
[06:46] Maya: Quick nit — our security team will need the SOC2 and encryption architecture doc.
[06:50] Alex: Noted. I'll attach them to the follow-up.
[06:54] Jordan: Anything else on the contract? Are there termination or scale-down clauses for reserved nodes?
[06:59] Alex: Standard reserved contracts have minimum terms, but we can include flexible ramp clauses for the pilot. We'll surface options in the template.
[07:07] Rosa: Can you also confirm whether audit logs show token-level request ids? We need traceability to source requests.
[07:13] Priya: Yes, we can surface request IDs, user identity mapping, and model version in logs. Data retention is configurable.
[07:21] Jordan: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[07:24] Alex: Recap — Alex will send pricing + security docs, Priya will scope benchmark, KilnWorks will share payloads and compliance contacts, and we'll schedule pilot kickoff after benchmark review.
[07:36] Ethan: One more quick thing - for the nightly spike, could we test a hybrid strategy: a prewarm layer plus transient overprovisioning?
[07:43] Priya: Absolutely; we'll model hybrid strategies in the perf tests.
[07:48] Jordan: Thanks all. Appreciate the clarity.
[07:50] Alex: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with the packet and next steps.
[07:53] End of recording: 00:48:12 (approx)
